newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Little easing if new pension adopted RB tells NZPA.
newsitem.headline: Little easing if new pension adopted RB tells NZPA.

text.p: Any easing in monetary policy following a yes vote in September's compulsory Retirement Savings Scheme (RSS) referendum would be small, Reserve Bank chief manager of financial markets David Archer said on Monday.

He told the New Zealand Press Association in an interview that back of envelope calculations by the bank suggested that a yes vote would not be a big deal for either inflation pressures or monetary policy.
"We are doing some back of envelope figuring of what the impact of an RSS would be and the basic conclusion is the effects are going to be small," Archer said.
The scheme being promoted by the Government would involve contributions rising to 8 percent of income over five years, largely funded from previously announced tax cuts.
Archer said the tax cuts by themselves would add around half a percent to the inflation rate if the bank did not react with policy.
"If you put the RSS in as well the impact of the tax cuts on inflation pressures is probably close to being halved.

"We are talking about less than a quarter of a percent (impact) on the inflation rate. That's something. So yes, we could have slightly easier monetary policy than we have got built into the projections but the numbers are not large.
"The overall impact on future monetary policy is not a big deal," he said.

Polls currently suggest that a yes vote is unlikely in the postal ballot to be run from September 5 to 26. The central bank assumed no change to superannuation policy in its June monetary policy statement and that policy was expected to be unchanged in the bank's September economic projections statement due on September 18.
Archer said the bank may produce an alternative scenario in its September statement which would incorporate the impact of a yes vote but no decision has yet been made on this.

Economists have suggested that a yes vote, which would divert the $1.02 billion of tax cuts due on July 1, 1998 into the RSS would allow the bank to run an easier monetary policy because people would spend less, reducing inflation pressures. It could also reduce growth.
Archer did not comment specifically on the impact a yes vote would have on growth.
Treasurer Winston Peters last month rejected concerns that RSS would slow down growth in a testimony to Parliament's finance and expenditure committee.
However, he told the committee that policy judgements by the Reserve Bank would have to be made if there was a yes vote, and that would impact on the growth rate.
He also said the impact on growth would depend on where fund managers invested the money.
Treasury made general comments about the impact of the RSS in the budget delivered on June 26 before the detail of the RSS scheme was known.

It said then that "while an increase in household savings would tend to reduce consumption in the short term, this does not mean that economic growth will be lower. As a result of less demand pressure in the economy, inflation pressures would likely to be weaker. This will allow monetary conditions to be easier."
Underlying inflation was 1.49 percent in the June quarter, around the middle of the Reserve Bank's zero to 3 percent target band.
